## 1 Need for a Package Handling Complex Variable Dependencies in Multivariate Time Series

Building predictive diagnostic models for multivariate time series often begins with feature selection. A standard machine learning reflex is to compute a linear correlation matrix to identify and drop redundant variables. While useful for simple stochastic processes, this linear assumption frequently breaks down in physical domains.

In industrial Internet of Things (IoT) environments, for example, variables are governed by causal, closed-loop mechanics. To illustrate this, we load the `hvac_features` dataset (Turin HVAC telemetry [@borda2022development]) provided with `isoRouting` and examine the linear correlation across its 11 telemetry channels.


```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Loading Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(isoRouting)

# Load the bundled package data
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# Restrict to raw variables (the package data also contains engineered features)
hvac_raw <- hvac_features |> 
  select(
    t_supply, t_return, sp_return, t_saturation, t_outdoor, 
    rh_supply, rh_return, rh_outdoor, energy, power
  )

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| code-summary: "Correlation Heatmap Code"
#| fig-cap: "Global Pearson correlation heatmap (Turin HVAC Raw Telemetry)"

library(ggcorrplot)

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(hvac_raw, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Set the diagonal to NA to de-emphasize trivial self-correlations
diag(cor_matrix) <- NA

# Generate the square ggplot-based heatmap
ggcorrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "square",
  type = "full",
  lab = TRUE,              
  lab_size = 3.5,
  lab_col = "black",       
  colors = c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4"), 
  outline.color = "gray90",
  legend.title = "Correlation"
) +
theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
  axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold")
) +
scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)
```

Based on the heatmap one could be tempted to remove some variables with high correlation. However, examining the raw pairwise dependencies reveals a much more complex geometric reality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pairs-plot
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Scatterplot Code"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Scatterplot matrix with correlation-mapped backgrounds (Sampled at n = 5000)"

library(GGally)

# 1. Custom function to calculate correlation and map it to a background color
custom_scatter_bg <- function(data, mapping, ...) {
  x_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$x)
  y_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$y)
  
  corr <- cor(x_data, y_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  
  color_fun <- colorRamp(c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4")) 
  scaled_corr <- (corr + 1) / 2 
  
  rgb_vec <- color_fun(scaled_corr)
  hex_color <- rgb(rgb_vec[1], rgb_vec[2], rgb_vec[3], maxColorValue = 255)
  
  ggplot(data, mapping) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, 
             fill = hex_color, alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(...)
}

# 2. Generate the plot for a sample using the restricted raw data
set.seed(42)
p_pairs <- hvac_raw |>
  sample_n(5000) |> 
  ggpairs(
    lower = list(continuous = wrap(custom_scatter_bg, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5)),
    upper = list(continuous = wrap(custom_scatter_bg, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5)),
    title = "Pairwise Scatterplot Matrix (HVAC Raw Telemetry)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA)
  )

p_pairs
```

The scatterplot matrix shows that linear correlation is an inadequate measure here. Variables form distinct geometric manifolds, dense operational clusters, and hard boundaries dictated by mechanical limits and programmed setpoints.   

Explicitly modeling these dependencies using traditional parametric methods requires a prohibitive expansion of interaction terms, quickly rendering models unmanageable.

This geometric complexity is why `isoRouting` utilizes the Isolation Forest algorithm [@liu2008isolation]. Rather than attempting to explicitly model the dense, intricate topology of "normal" operations, the Isolation Forest uses non-Euclidean random partitioning to efficiently isolate anomalies that fall outside these manifolds.

To make anomaly detection actionable in an operations research context, isoRouting establishes a two-tiered diagnostic framework that decouples system explanation from operational alerting:

- **Archetype Discovery (Explaining Faults)**: By capturing a broad statistical substrate of anomalous time courses, the engine provides sufficient data density to map distinct operational manifolds. Clustering this substrate yields spatial medoids—the representative profiles of deviations from nominal variable interactions. Rather than classifying every point in this subset as a critical failure, these archetypes are used to map the distinct operating regions associated with anomalous behavior.
- **Threshold Triggers (Alerting on Severity)**: Once underlying behavioral departures are established, a high anomaly score threshold governs active alerts. When an extreme alert fires, its proximity to a pre-computed medoid associates it with a known fault archetype, enabling rapid root-cause diagnosis or the flagging of novel anomalies.

## 2 Engine Workflow

The `isoRouting` package is built around the `DiagnosticEngine`, a state-based S4 class designed to enforce a sequential workflow. The engine tracks its internal state , ensuring that prerequisites—such as data ingestion, anomaly scoring, and topological distance computation—are completed in the correct order before advanced diagnostic or routing methods can be executed.

### 2.1 Execution Lifecycle

The chronological lifecycle of the `DiagnosticEngine`, from uninitialized configuration to committed forensic ledgers, is outlined in @tbl-engine-workflow.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-engine-workflow
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-summary: "Workflow Table Code"

library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

workflow_summary <- data.frame(
  Step = 1:7,
  Method = c(
    "`initialize(config_path)`",
    "`ingest_time_course(data)`",
    "`extract_anomalies(threshold)`",
    "`compute_distances()`",
    "`calibrate(min_k, max_k)`",
    "`extract_medoids(k)`",
    "`commit_ledger()` / `route_time_course()`"
  ),
  Starting_State = c(
    "Uninitialized",
    "Initialized",
    "Time Course Ingested",
    "Anomalies Extracted",
    "Distances Computed",
    "Calibrated",
    "Medoids Extracted"
  ),
  Resulting_State = c(
    "Initialized",
    "Time Course Ingested",
    "Anomalies Extracted",
    "Distances Computed",
    "Calibrated",
    "Medoids Extracted",
    "Ledger Committed"
  ),
  Operational_Purpose = c(
    "Parses the YAML schema, target variables, and machine learning hyperparameters.",
    "Validates timestamps, enforces temporal continuity, and isolates target variables.",
    "Trains the Isolation Forest model, scores the entire time course, and filters extreme events.",
    "Extracts terminal leaf nodes and computes the size-agnostic proportional Hamming distance matrix.",
    "Applies divisive hierarchical clustering (DIANA) across k-values to maximize global silhouette width.",
    "Identifies physical time-series archetypes (medoids) and computes empirical cluster radii (event horizons).",
    "Ranks historical anomalies by distance to medoid, or projects the full time series to track sub-threshold evolution."
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(
  workflow_summary, 
  col.names = c("Step", "Engine Method", "Input State", "Output State", "Operational Purpose"),
  caption = "Chronological execution lifecycle and state transitions of the DiagnosticEngine S4 class."
)
```

## 3 Example of Workflow with Non-Engineered Features

We first illustrate `isoRouting` using a "naive" configuration built strictly on the 10 raw telemetry channels of the Turin HVAC dataset. Omitting dynamic feature engineering will provide a baseline that highlights why encoding temporal rates of change is essential for time-series anomaly routing.

### 3.1 Data Preparation and Temporal Integrity

The first step in the `isoRouting` pipeline is preparing the time-course data. Because the engine's core methods rely on regular time intervals, `DiagnosticEngine` requires a properly formatted datetime column named `timestamp` (`POSIXt`).

We begin by loading the Turin HVAC dataset bundled with the package and verifying the `timestamp` column class:

```{r}
#| label: data-ingestion
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Loading Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(isoRouting)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# Load the package-associated Turin HVAC dataset
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# Verify the timestamp column is present and properly classed
class(hvac_features$timestamp)
```

Before initializing the engine, we scan the dataset for missing periods using `check_time_continuity()`:

```{r}
#| label: continuity-check
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Continuity Check Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Evaluate temporal continuity
continuity_check <- check_time_continuity(hvac_features$timestamp)

# Truncate gap_indices for display while printing the full interval summary
print(modifyList(continuity_check, list(
  gap_indices = c(head(continuity_check$gap_indices, 16), "...")
)))
```

The output of `check_time_continuity()` returns a boolean continuity flag alongside a frequency table of all intervals between consecutive `timestamps`. While the standard polling interval for the Turin HVAC system is 900 seconds (15 minutes), `$summary` reveals a major discontinuity of 15,814,800 seconds (approximately 6 months), alongside several minor outages ranging from a few hours to six days.

Ingesting a 6-month gap would severely distort estimations performed by `isoRouting`. However, the underlying Isolation Forest and distance matrices can handle minor maintenance downtimes without requiring synthetic data imputation.

Therefore, we will split the dataset into two distinct periods across the 6-month boundary. We will use both early and late segments for different purposes in this vignette. We also verify that both segments are continuous within a 7-day tolerance.

```{r}
#| label: data-split-and-validation
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Split Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Calculate time differences to locate the 6-month gap
time_diffs <- as.numeric(difftime(
  hvac_features$timestamp[-1], 
  hvac_features$timestamp[-nrow(hvac_features)], 
  units = "secs"
))

# Locate the index of the largest gap (6-month shutdown)
major_gap_idx <- which.max(time_diffs)

# Bucket 1: Pre-Gap (~40% of data)
baseline_telemetry <- hvac_features |> 
  slice(1:major_gap_idx)

# Bucket 2: Post-Gap (~60% of data)
stream_telemetry <- hvac_features |> 
  slice((major_gap_idx + 1):n())

# Validate both buckets using a 7-day tolerance (604,800 seconds)
baseline_check <- check_time_continuity(baseline_telemetry$timestamp, 
                                        tolerance = 604800)
stream_check   <- check_time_continuity(stream_telemetry$timestamp, 
                                        tolerance = 604800)

if (!baseline_check$is_continuous || !stream_check$is_continuous) {
  stop("One or both  buckets contain large time discontinuities.")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "Continuity verified (7-day tolerance): Baseline (%d rows) and Stream (%d rows).\n",
    nrow(baseline_telemetry), nrow(stream_telemetry)
  ))
}
```

### 3.2 Engine Configuration and Initialization

The `DiagnosticEngine` uses a YAML configuration file to define its model parameters and feature schema[cite: 2, 3]. We start with a naive configuration that passes the raw sensor readings directly to the model[cite: 3].

In `isoRouting`, the schema divides variables into two categories[cite: 3]:

- **Target Variables:** Variables used by the Isolation Forest to score anomalies and compute forest-based distances[cite: 3].
- **Context Variables:** Variables excluded from the model, but retained within the extracted medoid time windows for visual interpretation[cite: 3].

In this naive setup, we assign all 10 temperature, humidity, energy, and power channels as target variables and leave the context variables empty[cite: 3]. We then instantiate the S4 object with `new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = ...)`[cite: 3].

```{r}
#| label: naive-initialization
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Configuration and Instantiation Code"

# Define the naive YAML schema using raw sensor values
yaml_naive <- "
ntrees: 500
sample_size: 256
temporal_window_hours: 2
anomaly_threshold: 0.60
context_variables: []
target_variables:
  - t_supply
  - t_return
  - sp_return
  - t_saturation
  - t_outdoor
  - rh_supply
  - rh_return
  - rh_outdoor
  - energy
  - power
"

# Write the configuration to a temporary file for ingestion
config_naive <- tempfile(pattern = "naive_config_", fileext = ".yml")
writeLines(yaml_naive, config_naive)

# Instantiate the DiagnosticEngine
engine <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_naive)

# Verify the target and context variables parsed from the schema
get_features(engine)
```

### 3.3 Time Course Ingestion

Next, we load the baseline dataset into the S4 object using `ingest_time_course()`. This method verifies that the `timestamp` column is properly formatted and that all `target_variables` from the YAML schema exist in the input data frame. It also drops any columns not listed as target or context variables before storing the validated time course in the engine.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-time-course
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Ingestion Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Ingest the historical baseline telemetry into the engine
engine <- ingest_time_course(engine, data = baseline_telemetry)

# Verify the updated lifecycle state of the engine
engine@domain_state

# Inspect the ingested data structure (features not listed in the YAML are dropped)
glimpse(get_time_course(engine))
```

### 3.4 Anomaly Extraction via Isolation Forest

With the time course ingested, we run `extract_anomalies()` to score the dataset and isolate extreme events[cite: 2, 3].

The `DiagnosticEngine` uses an Isolation Forest (`isotree`) to score the target variables[cite: 2, 3]. Rather than relying on geometric distances, Isolation Forests partition the data by randomly selecting a variable and a split value[cite: 3]. Because anomalies are rare and distinct, they require fewer splits to isolate, resulting in shorter path lengths in the decision trees and higher anomaly scores (scaled between 0 and 1)[cite: 3].

Using the YAML parameters (`ntrees: 500`, `sample_size: 256`), the engine trains the forest, scores the full baseline time course, and stores observations with scores at or above the `0.60` threshold in the `@anomalies` slot[cite: 2, 3].

```{r}
#| label: extract-anomalies
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Anomaly Extraction Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Score the feature space and extract extreme events
engine <- extract_anomalies(engine)

# Verify the engine state
engine@domain_state

# Check how many observations exceeded the 0.60 threshold
nrow(engine@anomalies)
```

### 3.5 Visualizing the Threshold Landscape

In practice, choosing an anomaly threshold does not have to be arbitrary. `isoRouting` provides two quick methods to explore the relationship between the anomaly score threshold ($T$) and the number of extracted events ($N$).

First, `explore_thresholds()` scores the feature space across a sequence of candidate cutoffs without altering the engine's internal state, allowing users to plot the decay curve of isolated events.

```{r}
#| label: naive-explore-thresholds
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Threshold Exploration Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Generate a threshold landscape for the ingested baseline telemetry
threshold_curve <- explore_thresholds(engine, thresholds = seq(0.50, 0.75, by = 0.01))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-threshold-decay
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Visualization Code"
#| fig-cap: "Anomaly threshold decay curve showing the reduction in isolated extreme events as the Isolation Forest score threshold increases."
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)

# Plot the decay of extreme events
ggplot(threshold_curve, aes(x = Threshold, y = Event_Count)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.60, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Anomaly Threshold Decay Curve",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the 0.60 YAML selection",
    x = "Isolation Forest Threshold",
    y = "Number of Extracted Events"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Conversely, get_threshold_at_N() finds the score cutoff required to isolate at least $N$ anomalies.

```{r}
#| label: get-threshold_at_N
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "get_threshold_at_N Call Code"

threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, 40)
cat(paste0("Threshold = ", signif(threshold, 3), " yields at least 40 anomalies\n"))
```

While these two methods map event counts to score cutoffs, they do not indicate whether the isolated events form meaningful clusters. To evaluate how clustering structure changes across thresholds, `isoRouting` provides the `evaluate_k_stability()` diagnostic method presented next.

### 3.6 Threshold Diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: naive-evaluate-stability
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show evaluate_k_stability Call"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Sweep based on statistical substrate size (N)
stability_curve_naive <- evaluate_k_stability(engine, max_N = 800, min_N = 20, nb_steps = 61, max_k = 10)
```

Method `evaluate_k_stability()` maps the anomaly threshold against three independent diagnostics. Note that the engine does not utilize Euclidean or isolation-forest (`isotree`, sample-size dependent) distances between anomalies. Instead, `isoRouting` uses a **proportional Hamming distance**: the fraction of trees in the forest where two observations land in *different* terminal leaves. This metric measures structural disagreement and is independent of the number of anomalies. 

- **Optimal Clusters ($k$)**: At each value of threshold $\theta$, divisive clustering [@kaufman1990finding] is utilized to group anomalies. The optimal number $k$ of clusters (best tree cut) is then defined as the one maximizing the global silhouette score [@rousseeuw1987silhouettes]. Visualization of $k$ as a function of $\theta$ helps identify $\theta$ intervals where clustering is stable.
- **Hartigan's Dip Statistic ($D$)**: The statistic (effect size) of a non-parametric test applied to the Hamming distance matrix. A peak in $D$ rejects the hypothesis of unimodality, indicating maximum distance heterogeneity (i.e., the likely presence of highly distinct clusters) [@hartigan1985dip].
- **Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)**: Measures how many variables remain independent. A decrease in LID suggests a system "breakdown," where variables become more coupled due to a physical fault (e.g. a sensor break will decrease variance of a variable).

<b id="stability-ggplot-target" class="flash-target">Diagnostics Plotting Wrapper</b>
```{r}
#| label: stability-ggplot-function
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show ggplot Function"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Define a reusable plotting wrapper
plot_topological_stability <- function(stability_df, plot_title, plot_subtitle) {
  
  # Pivot the profile dataframe for multi-panel plotting
  plot_data <- stability_df |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c(N_Anomalies, Opt_k, Hartigans_D, Global_LID), 
      names_to = "Metric", 
      values_to = "Value"
    ) |>
    mutate(Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("N_Anomalies", "Hartigans_D", "Global_LID", "Opt_k")))
  
  # Identify the maximum Hartigan's D for highlighting
  max_dip <- plot_data |>
    filter(Metric == "Hartigans_D") |>
    filter(Value == max(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    slice(1)
  
  # Identify the minimum LID for highlighting
  min_lid <- plot_data |>
    filter(Metric == "Global_LID") |>
    filter(Value == min(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    slice(1)
  
  # Plot the 4-panel stability profile
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Threshold, y = Value, color = Metric)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_point(data = max_dip, fill = "gold", color = "red", size = 4, shape = 21, stroke = 1.2) +
    geom_point(data = min_lid, fill = "gold", color = "red", size = 4, shape = 21, stroke = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(
      ~Metric, 
      scales = "free_y", 
      ncol = 1,
      labeller = as_labeller(c(
        N_Anomalies = "Number of Anomalies (N)",
        Hartigans_D = "Cluster Effect Size (Hartigan's Dip Statistic)", 
        Global_LID = "Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)",
        Opt_k = "Optimal Clusters (k)"
      ))
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
      "N_Anomalies" = "#0072B2", 
      "Hartigans_D" = "#009E73", 
      "Global_LID" = "#CC79A7", 
      "Opt_k" = "#D55E00"
    )) +
    scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Threshold",
      y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), 
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-evaluate-stability
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Plot Call"

#| fig-height: 12

#| warning: false

# Generate the Naive Plot
fig_naive <- plot_topological_stability(
  stability_curve_naive,
  plot_title = "Anomaly Threshold Diagnostics: Naive Configuration",
  plot_subtitle = "Mapping cluster plateaus (k), distance heterogeneity (D), and variable dependencies breaks (LID) to guide threshold exploration."
)

print(fig_naive)
```

@fig-naive-evaluate-stability shows candidate plateaus at $k = 4$, $k=3$ and $k=2$. We choose to ignore the plateau at $k=4$ because, while it spans the largest threshold interval, it still represents at least 200 points and its metrics $D$ and LID are not remarkable. The plateau at $k=2$ starts with the maximum $D$ value, indicating at least two very different types of distances in the Hamming matrix. The last small plateau at $k=3$ is also interesting because it indicates severe breakdown due to its small LID value.

Comparing values of diagnostic metrics $D$ and LID is in itself useful. One can also ask the following question: are those values "significantly" large or small? Answering such questions requires building null models of these two metrics. We start with metric $D$ by utilizing the helper function `simulate_dip_control`.

```{r}
#| label: naive-anomaly-thresholds
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Null Dip Computation"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

n_sequence <- seq(20, 100, by = 10)

dip_control_naive <- map_dfr(n_sequence, function(n) {
  res <- simulate_dip_control(engine, N = n, iterations = 200)
  res$Threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, n)
  return(res)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-null-dip

library(ggplot2)

# Define a reusable plotting wrapper for all null profiles
plot_baseline_profile <- function(results_df, line_color, plot_title, plot_subtitle, y_label) {
  ggplot(results_df, aes(x = Threshold)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), fill = line_color, alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = Median), color = line_color, linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(aes(y = Median), color = line_color, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Threshold",
      y = y_label
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-control-dip
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Plot Call"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated Control Bounds of Hartigan's Dip Statistic. The observed peak in the actual stability profile far exceeds the 95% threshold, rejecting the possibility of the observed peak being an artifact of the Hamming distance matrix. Irregular sampling of the threshold is explained by mapping the grid directly to the number of anomalies (N)."

# Generate the Naive Dip Plot
fig_dip_null_naive <- plot_baseline_profile(
  dip_control_naive,
  line_color = "#D55E00", 
  plot_title = "Control Quantiles for Hartigan's D (Naive Configuration)",
  plot_subtitle = "Median and [5%, 95%] bounds estimated with Monte Carlo simulations.",
  y_label = "Hartigan's D"
)

print(fig_dip_null_naive)
```

@fig-naive-control-dip displays quantiles of a control distribution for $D$ obtained with the following simulation scheme at each value of $N$: we uniformly sample $N$ observations directly from the entire ingested time course, construct the a Hamming distance matrix for that subset, and compute Hartigan's $D$.

Repeated across Monte Carlo iterations, this establishes a baseline of expected distance heterogeneity. By sampling primarily from nominal operations, and not anomalies, the simulation preserves the multivariate dependencies of the dataset. This yields a conservative control to test whether the extracted anomalies exhibit greater distance heterogeneity than typical system variance.

In @fig-naive-evaluate-stability, we observed a maximum $D$ of approximately 0.06 near $T = 0.653$. In the control plot, the 95th percentile of the control distribution remains below 0.045 across the entire sweep. This gap holds at all values of $N$, confirming that the distance heterogeneity observed in the anomaly matrix is a structural property of the faults, not a mathematical artifact.

```{r}
#| label: naive-null-lid-profile-preparation
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Show Data Preparation (call to simulation helper)"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# Sweep the Monte Carlo simulation for the Naive Engine
# Reusing the n_sequence defined in the previous Dip chunk
lid_results_naive <- map_dfr(n_sequence, function(n) {
  res <- simulate_lid_control(engine, N = n, iterations = 200)
  res$Threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, n)
  return(res)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lid-control
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Show Plot Call"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated Control Bounds for Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The observed dimensionality of the anomalies falls far below the 5% lower bound, confirming a severe structural break (variable coupling) during fault states."

message(sprintf("Simulating random healthy LID space across %d steps...", length(n_sequence)))

fig_lid_naive <- plot_baseline_profile(
  lid_results_naive,
  line_color = "#CC79A7", 
  plot_title = "Control Quantiles for Intrinsic Dimensionality (Naive Configuration)",

  y_label = "Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)"
```
